facts.claim: Index insurance pays out benefits on the basis of a predetermined index, such as rainfall level, without requiring the traditional services of insurance claims assessors.
facts.source_title: Insurance (IFC Financial Inclusion page, includes FAQ: Index Insurance from the Global Index Insurance Facility)
facts.publisher: International Finance Corporation (World Bank Group), Global Index Insurance Facility
facts.quote: pays out benefits on the basis of a predetermined index (e.g. rainfall level) for loss of assets and investments, primarily working capital, resulting from weather and catastrophic events
facts.checker_quote: Index insurance is a relatively new but innovative approach to insurance provision that pays out benefits on the basis of a predetermined index (e.g. rainfall level) for loss of assets and investments, primarily working capital, resulting from weather and catastrophic events.
facts.checker_note: The predetermined index part is confirmed on the live page. The page never says payouts are made 'rather than according to an assessment of each farmer's actual loss'. The nearest wording is 'without requiring the traditional services of insurance claims assessors', and elsewhere it says index measurements may not match an individual insured's actual losses. The contrast is implied, not stated. The World Bank 2011 paper (claims 4 to 8) does state it directly: 'Because no field loss assessment is made under index insurance, the payout is based entirely on the index measurement'. That paper would be a better source for the claim as written.

facts.claim: The index is set before the insurance period starts and tracks how far conditions such as rainfall or temperature move away from normal levels.
facts.source_title: Insurance (IFC Financial Inclusion page, includes FAQ: Index Insurance from the Global Index Insurance Facility)
facts.publisher: International Finance Corporation (World Bank Group), Global Index Insurance Facility
facts.quote: Before the start of the insurance period, a statistical index is developed. The index measures deviations from the normal level of parameters such as rainfall, temperature
facts.checker_quote: Before the start of the insurance period, a statistical index is developed. The index measures deviations from the normal level of parameters such as rainfall, temperature, earthquake magnitude, wind speed, crop yield, or livestock mortality rates.
facts.checker_note: Matches the live page word for word.

facts.claim: Because index insurance does not necessarily require the traditional services of insurance claims assessors, claims can be settled faster and more objectively.
facts.source_title: Insurance (IFC Financial Inclusion page, includes FAQ: Index Insurance from the Global Index Insurance Facility)
facts.publisher: International Finance Corporation (World Bank Group), Global Index Insurance Facility
facts.quote: Because index insurance does not necessarily require the traditional services of insurance claims assessors, it allows for the claims settlement processes to be quicker and more objective.
facts.checker_quote: Because index insurance does not necessarily require the traditional services of insurance claims assessors, it allows for the claims settlement processes to be quicker and more objective.
facts.checker_note: The source hedges with 'does not necessarily require'. The claim says flatly 'does not need' and adds 'to visit farms', which the page does not say. The corrected wording keeps the hedge. A summary paragraph higher on the same page says 'without requiring the traditional services of insurance claims assessors', so the page is not consistent with itself. The hedged FAQ wording is the safer one to follow.

facts.claim: In a traditional crop insurance contract, payouts follow a loss assessment made after the event, while an index contract uses a payout scale agreed in advance that sets how much is paid for each unit of the weather measure.
facts.source_title: Weather Index Insurance for Agriculture: Guidance for Development Practitioners (Agriculture and Rural Development Discussion Paper 50)
facts.publisher: World Bank
facts.quote: In a traditional contract, the insurer will price the contract based mainly on probabilistic models, and payouts will be made in accordance to an ex-post loss assessment. For indexbased contracts, however, it is necessary to agree to an ex-ante payout scale
facts.checker_quote: In a traditional contract, the insurer will price the contract based mainly on probabilistic models, and payouts will be made in accordance to an ex-post loss assessment. For indexbased contracts, however, it is necessary to agree to an ex-ante payout scale that will determine how much the contract will pay for each unit of weather variable.
facts.checker_note: Confirmed in the extracted PDF text, under 'Trigger payout levels'. The cover reads Agriculture and Rural Development Discussion Paper 50, November 2011. The source says 'traditional contract' in an agricultural insurance context, so 'traditional crop insurance contract' is a fair reading.

facts.claim: Removing field loss assessment cuts running costs, because traditional crop insurance has to send out large numbers of trained assessors.
facts.source_title: Weather Index Insurance for Agriculture: Guidance for Development Practitioners (Agriculture and Rural Development Discussion Paper 50)
facts.publisher: World Bank
facts.quote: The ability of index insurance to make payouts without field assessment clearly reduces administrative costs by eliminating the need for assessors.
facts.checker_quote: Field loss assessment is eliminated. Loss assessment is a challenge for any traditional crop insurance program, because of the need to mobilize large numbers of skilled or semiskilled assessors who possess some agronomic knowledge. The ability of index insurance to make payouts without field assessment clearly reduces administrative costs by eliminating the need for assessors.
facts.checker_note: Supported in substance. The source says 'administrative costs' and 'skilled or semiskilled assessors who possess some agronomic knowledge', not 'running costs' and 'trained assessors'. The corrected wording follows the source more closely. The quote in the task covers only the last sentence. The 'large numbers' part comes from the sentence before it, which is now included above.

facts.claim: Because the payout depends on an independent weather measurement and not on what happens on the farm, farmers cannot influence the claim, which reduces moral hazard.
facts.source_title: Weather Index Insurance for Agriculture: Guidance for Development Practitioners (Agriculture and Rural Development Discussion Paper 50)
facts.publisher: World Bank
facts.quote: With index insurance, farmers have no ability or incentive to influence the claim, since payout is based on an independent and exogenous weather parameter, independent of farmers' behavior.
facts.checker_quote: Reduced moral hazard. In traditional insurance farmers may be able to influence the claim (by exacerbating physical losses) through their behavior, a phenomenon referred to as moral hazard. With index insurance, farmers have no ability or incentive to influence the claim, since payout is based on an independent and exogenous weather parameter, independent of farmers' behavior.
facts.checker_note: Confirmed in the extracted PDF text. The source ties the payout to farmers' behavior, not to 'what happens on the farm'. The paraphrase is close enough.

facts.claim: All farmers in a defined area buy on the same terms and payout scale, which the World Bank says virtually eliminates adverse selection for insurers.
facts.source_title: Weather Index Insurance for Agriculture: Guidance for Development Practitioners (Agriculture and Rural Development Discussion Paper 50)
facts.publisher: World Bank
facts.quote: farmers subscribe based on the terms, conditions, and payout scale for all farmers in their defined area, virtually eliminating the adverse selection problem for insurers.
facts.checker_quote: An advantage of index insurance is that farmers subscribe based on the terms, conditions, and payout scale for all farmers in their defined area, virtually eliminating the adverse selection problem for insurers.
facts.checker_note: Confirmed in the extracted PDF text, under 'Reduced risk of adverse selection'. It is a World Bank discussion paper, so 'the World Bank says' is a fair attribution. The paper's own disclaimers may say it does not necessarily reflect official World Bank views. I did not check that, so 'a World Bank paper says' is the safer wording.

facts.claim: The main trade-off is basis risk, the gap between what the index pays and what the farmer actually lost, and the World Bank calls it the most problematic feature of index insurance.
facts.source_title: Weather Index Insurance for Agriculture: Guidance for Development Practitioners (Agriculture and Rural Development Discussion Paper 50)
facts.publisher: World Bank
facts.quote: Basis risk is the most problematic feature of index insurance. It is the difference between the payout as measured by the index and the actual loss incurred by the farmer.
facts.checker_quote: Basis risk. Basis risk is the most problematic feature of index insurance. It is the difference between the payout as measured by the index and the actual loss incurred by the farmer.
facts.checker_note: Confirmed in the extracted PDF text. 'Main trade-off' is the claim's own framing. The source says 'most problematic feature', and the claim also quotes that correctly. The attribution caution from claim 7 applies here too.

facts.claim: Because the trigger matches losses only imperfectly, index insurance can pay in years when there are no losses and fail to pay in years when there are.
facts.source_title: How to Measure Whether Index Insurance Provides Reliable Protection (Policy Research Working Paper 7744), by Karlijn Morsink, Daniel Jonathan Clarke and Shadreck Mapfumo
facts.publisher: World Bank Group, Finance and Markets Global Practice
facts.quote: index insurance provides claim payments based on a trigger that is only imperfectly correlated with losses. This implies that it carries basis risk: it may provide claim payments in years when there are no losses, and no claim payments in years when there are losses.
facts.checker_quote: However, index insurance provides claim payments based on a trigger that is only imperfectly correlated with losses. This implies that it carries basis risk: it may provide claim payments in years when there are no losses, and no claim payments in years when there are losses.
facts.checker_note: Confirmed in the abstract in the extracted PDF text. Title, authors (Karlijn Morsink, Daniel Jonathan Clarke, Shadreck Mapfumo), Policy Research Working Paper 7744, Finance and Markets Global Practice Group and July 2016 all match the cover.

facts.claim: Basis risk grows with the distance between the weather station or satellite measurement and the farm, so denser stations and finer satellite pixels help reduce it.
facts.source_title: Insurance (IFC Financial Inclusion page, includes FAQ: Index Insurance from the Global Index Insurance Facility)
facts.publisher: International Finance Corporation (World Bank Group), Global Index Insurance Facility
facts.quote: The greater the distance between the measurement instrument and the field, the greater the basis risk. Some households that experience loss may not receive compensation while others that experience no loss may receive payments.
facts.checker_quote: Geographical basis risk is a factor of the distance between the index measurement location and the production field. The greater the distance between the measurement instrument and the field, the greater the basis risk. ... Basis risk is reduced when the area covered by the index is homogeneous both in terms of weather and in terms of farming techniques. Therefore, as the density of weather stations and satellite pixels is increased, basis risk is minimized.
facts.checker_note: Supported in substance on the live page. The source speaks of geographical basis risk and 'the measurement instrument and the field', not 'weather station or satellite measurement and the farm'. It says 'density of weather stations and satellite pixels', not 'finer pixels'. The corrected wording follows the source. The quote in the task is from the same passage, but it leaves out the sentence about stations and pixels, which is the part that supports the second half of the claim.

facts.claim: Basis risk in index insurance is the chance that the index reading does not match the actual loss on a farmer's own field.
facts.source_title: What is basis risk? (FAQ)
facts.publisher: Global Index Insurance Facility (now Global Inclusive Insurance Facility), World Bank Group
facts.quote: Basis risk in index insurance arises when the index measurements do not match an individual insured’s actual losses.
facts.checker_quote: Basis risk in index insurance arises when the index measurements do not match an individual insured's actual losses.
facts.checker_note: The page loaded and contains this sentence. The site is branded Index Insurance Forum with a footer reading GIIF and refers to the Global Inclusive Insurance Facility. I did not see the World Bank Group named on the page itself, so the publisher line should not rely on this page for that.

facts.claim: Because payouts follow an index rather than an assessed loss, a policy can pay in a year with no losses and fail to pay in a year when farmers do lose crops.
facts.source_title: How to Measure Whether Index Insurance Provides Reliable Protection (Policy Research Working Paper 7744), Morsink, Clarke and Mapfumo
facts.publisher: World Bank Group, Finance and Markets Global Practice
facts.quote: it may provide claim payments in years when there are no losses, and no claim payments in years when there are losses.
facts.checker_quote: However, index insurance provides claim payments based on a trigger that is only imperfectly correlated with losses. This implies that it carries basis risk: it may provide claim payments in years when there are no losses, and no claim payments in years when there are losses.
facts.checker_note: Found in the abstract of Policy Research Working Paper 7744, Morsink, Clarke and Mapfumo, Finance and Markets Global Practice Group, July 2016. The same idea is repeated in the introduction and conclusion.

facts.claim: Basis risk can never be fully removed, because an index built from rainfall, vegetation or area yields estimates the average loss in an area, not the loss of each farmer.
facts.source_title: An Audit Rule to Protect Farmers in Case an Insurance Index Fails (Innovation Lab for Assets and Market Access Spotlight)
facts.publisher: Feed the Future Innovation Lab for Assets and Market Access, UC Davis (USAID funded)
facts.quote: An index of these factors predicts average losses in an area, not individual losses.
facts.checker_quote: This is beacuse index insurance links payouts to outside factors, such as levels of rainfall, vegetation growth or an area's average crop yields rather verified individual claims. An index of these factors predicts average losses in an area, not individual losses. For this reason, index insurance will always carry basis risk
facts.checker_note: The PDF is the AMA Innovation Lab Spotlight dated November 2017. The typos (beacuse, rather verified) are in the original. 'Always carry basis risk' supports 'can never be fully removed'.

facts.claim: In a study of index-based livestock insurance in northern Kenya, the index cut herders' exposure to large shared losses by an average of 62.8%, but the benefit was limited because many losses were specific to individual households.
facts.source_title: Basis Risk and the Welfare Gains from Index Insurance: Evidence from Northern Kenya (MPRA Paper No. 59153), Jensen, Barrett and Mude
facts.publisher: Cornell University and International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI), via Munich Personal RePEc Archive
facts.quote: IBLI reduces exposure to covariate risk due to high loss events by an average of 62.8%. The benefits of reduced covariate risk exposure are relatively small, however, due to high exposure to seemingly mostly random idiosyncratic risk
facts.checker_quote: we find that IBLI reduces exposure to covariate risk due to high loss events by an average of 62.8%. The benefits of reduced covariate risk exposure are relatively small, however, due to high exposure to seemingly mostly random idiosyncratic risk
facts.checker_note: Confirmed in the abstract of MPRA Paper No. 59153, Jensen, Barrett and Mude, September 2014. 'Idiosyncratic risk' means risk specific to the individual household, so the claim is a fair plain-language reading. The corrected wording stays closer to the source, which says the benefits were 'relatively small' and the risk 'seemingly mostly random'.

facts.claim: The same northern Kenya study found that, depending on the region, insured herders were still left with an average of 62.3% to 76.7% of their original risk from high loss events.
facts.source_title: Basis Risk and the Welfare Gains from Index Insurance: Evidence from Northern Kenya (MPRA Paper No. 59153), Jensen, Barrett and Mude
facts.publisher: Cornell University and International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI), via Munich Personal RePEc Archive
facts.quote: Depending on covariate region, IBLI policy holders are left with an average of between 62.3% and 76.7% of their original risk due to high loss events.
facts.checker_quote: Depending on covariate region, IBLI policy holders are left with an average of between 62.3% and 76.7% of their original risk due to high loss events.
facts.checker_note: Exact match in the abstract. The numbers, the scope (by covariate region, high loss events) and the dates all match.

facts.claim: World Bank researchers warn that offering index insurance that does not reliably pay can damage the reputation of the donors, governments and companies behind it.
facts.source_title: How to Measure Whether Index Insurance Provides Reliable Protection (Policy Research Working Paper 7744), Morsink, Clarke and Mapfumo
facts.publisher: World Bank Group, Finance and Markets Global Practice
facts.quote: Offering unreliable index insurance may lead to high reputation risk for donors, governments, and the private sector.
facts.checker_quote: Offering unreliable index insurance may lead to high reputation risk for donors, governments, and the private sector.
facts.checker_note: The sentence appears in the abstract and in the conclusion. One small attribution point: two of the three authors (Clarke, Mapfumo) are listed at the World Bank Group, but the lead author Morsink is listed at the University of Oxford (CSAE). The corrected wording credits the World Bank working paper, which is safer. The source says 'may lead to high reputation risk', which is softer than 'can damage the reputation'.

facts.claim: Research in northern Kenya found that basis risk plays a major role in whether herders choose to buy index insurance at all.
facts.source_title: How basis risk and spatiotemporal adverse selection influence demand for index insurance: Evidence from northern Kenya, Jensen, Mude and Barrett, Food Policy vol. 74
facts.publisher: Food Policy (Elsevier), peer-reviewed; abstract on EconPapers
facts.quote: our findings indicate that basis risk and spatiotemporal adverse selection also play a major role in determining demand for IBLI.

facts.checker_note: The figures match. Context: these are difference-in-difference estimates of what households expected to do over the next three months, compared with uninsured households. facts.claim: NDVI (Normalized Difference Vegetation Index) is a satellite measure of green vegetation that always falls between minus one and plus one, where zero means no vegetation and values near plus one mean very dense green leaves.
facts.source_title: Measuring Vegetation (NDVI & EVI)
facts.publisher: NASA Earth Observatory
facts.quote: A zero means no vegetation and close to +1 (0.8 - 0.9) indicates the highest possible density of green leaves.
facts.checker_quote: Calculations of NDVI for a given pixel always result in a number that ranges from minus one (-1) to plus one (+1); however, no green leaves gives a value close to zero. A zero means no vegetation and close to +1 (0.8 - 0.9) indicates the highest possible density of green leaves.
facts.checker_note: The page also says that nearly all satellite vegetation indices use this difference formula, and that its result is called the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index. The page shows Published Aug 30, 2000 and Last Updated Nov 14, 2025. The quote given in the input covers only part of the claim, so a fuller quote is given here.

facts.claim: A dekad splits each month into three parts: the 1st to the 10th, the 11th to the 20th, and the 21st to the last day, so the third dekad can be longer or shorter than 10 days.
facts.source_title: Weather Index Insurance for Agriculture: Guidance for Development Practitioners, Annex footnote 26, PDF page 100
facts.publisher: World Bank
facts.quote: A "dekad" is a conventional way of dividing a month in three intervals.
facts.checker_quote: A "dekad" is a conventional way of dividing a month in three intervals. The first two dekads of each month go, respectively, from the first to the tenth day and from the eleventh to the twentieth day of the month in object, while the third dekad goes from the twenty-first to the last day of each month. Hence, the third dekad may be composed of more or less than 10 days.
facts.checker_note: Found in footnote 26 of Annex 7 (WRSI technical note) on PDF page 100 (printed page 87). The full footnote supports every part of the claim.
